key: D minor → D major (written score; playback pitch unverified)
performers: Marian Anderson, contralto; San Francisco Symphony Orchestra; Pierre Monteux, conductor
question: Which parts of the storm’s motion survive when the music becomes a lullaby?
intro: The last song turns an orchestral storm into a lullaby. Repeated complaints about sending the children outside eventually give way to the image of shelter in their mother’s house; the orchestra carries the ending beyond the voice. This Marian Anderson–Pierre Monteux transfer is the comparison-only alternative.

sections.label: The storm subsides
sections.mNote: the texture thins and the pace broadens

sections.label: Lullaby · the last stanza
sections.mNote: the written tonic turns major around a quiet rocking figure

sections.label: Orchestral postlude
sections.mNote: instrumental lines continue after the singer’s final phrase

cues.title: A storm in fragments
cues.text: Short wind figures, string tremolos and accented harp chords crowd the opening. Follow the small repeated gestures rather than waiting for one long orchestral tune: the agitation comes from several layers moving together.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Song V, printed p. 60. The score identifies the layers; the report shows continuous activity from the opening. No individual attack is precisely aligned.

cues.title: Voice against the movement
cues.text: Across the storm stanzas, compare the singer’s declamation with the orchestra’s recurring figures. The words change from one protest to the next while the accompaniment repeatedly renews its pressure.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 60–77. The repeated-stanza writing and orchestral figures support this whole-passage listening task; no syllable is timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Weather in the poem
cues.text: Rückert repeatedly declares that he would never have sent the children out in such weather. The poem then admits that they have been carried away without his consent: the storm belongs to a bereaved parent’s speech, not to a documented event in Mahler’s life.
cues.evidence: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-lied-5-in-diesem-wetter/ Paraphrase of the German text, not a biographical account of a literal storm.

cues.title: The orchestra grows wider
cues.text: This song adds piccolo, contrabassoon and two further horns to the cycle’s resources. Those additions extend the top and bottom of the ensemble without introducing trumpets or trombones.
cues.evidence: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm Scoring list identifies piccolo and contrabassoon in song V only, with horns 3–4 also restricted to V. This cue describes the movement’s forces, not a timed entrance.

cues.title: Repetition under pressure
cues.text: Keep the opening rhythmic figures in mind through the later storm stanzas. Mahler can intensify familiar material by changing its register, density and dynamics rather than by giving the singer a wholly separate tune.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 68–77 show the continuing storm figures and successive stanzas. The comment is about the passage’s construction, not a measured tempo increase.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The weight falls away
cues.text: The storm’s accumulated sound drops into a much quieter stretch. Listen through the loss of weight before the next vocal span: the turn depends on withdrawal as well as on the melody that follows.
cues.evidence: The report shows level dropping from −8.1 dB at 2:40 to −26.9 dB at 2:55, before rising again at 3:05. This is the broad transition, not a precise final storm attack.

cues.title: Slow, like a lullaby
cues.text: The score now asks for “Langsam. Wie ein Wiegenlied” — slow, like a lullaby. A quiet rocking accompaniment replaces the storm’s compressed gestures; compare the changed motion with the earlier repeated figures.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 79. The level recovers gently around 3:05–3:20 after the deep 2:55–3:00 dip. This supports the approximate lullaby span, not its first syllable.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The chronology matters
cues.text: Mahler finishes the cycle in 1904, three years before his daughter Maria dies. Rückert’s words let him compose a bereaved parent’s voice before that loss; the songs were not written afterwards as a family memorial.
cues.evidence: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm gives the cycle’s composition years; the Mahler Foundation’s cycle introduction (https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/) records Maria’s death in 1907. No claim of premonition is made.

cues.title: Keep following the accompaniment
cues.text: Across the end of the lullaby and its postlude, listen beneath the upper line for the rocking inner figures. The instruments continue the sentence after the singer has no more words to add.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 83–86. Onset activity becomes very low from 4:30 onwards; the exact final vocal release is not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One inseparable cycle
cues.text: At the start of the score, Mahler asks that all five songs be treated as one inseparable whole and that interruptions, including applause, should not disturb their continuity. The final orchestral ending therefore closes the whole cycle, not merely a fifth independent song.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 3, composer’s footnote on continuity and applause.

cues.title: Sound before silence
cues.text: The final instrumental tones diminish before the file’s remaining silence. Listen to the release itself rather than treating the entire file tail as a continuing orchestral fade.
cues.evidence: The report shows −20.6 dB at 5:40, −40.5 dB at 5:45 and the −80 dB analysis floor from 5:50 through the 6:11 file end. The approximately twenty-second tail is not described as sounding music.

transitions.title: The storm releases its orchestral weight
transitions.how: The repeated storm figures lose their mass as Mahler slows the motion and reduces the active parts. A high held piccolo tone and the small bell’s repeated notes stand apart from the earlier crowded wind and string writing. This is a thinning bridge, not an abrupt cut to another song: the remaining figures carry the listener towards the lullaby.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 77–79. The sharp 2:40–2:55 level drop anchors the withdrawal. The exact entrance of piccolo or bell is not acoustically identified.

transitions.title: The repeated motion becomes rocking accompaniment
transitions.how: The notation turns from D minor towards D major and asks for a slow lullaby. Celesta and quiet string figures replace the storm’s harder attacks, while a sustained high tone links the textures. The final stanza keeps the weather imagery but changes its destination: the children are imagined at rest, and the orchestra’s continuing motion now rocks rather than drives.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 79 supplies the two-sharp signature and the lullaby marking. The renewed activity at 3:05 follows the transition’s deepest dip. Placement is provisional and not syllable-aligned. Key names describe the written score: this transfer’s final pitch classes are E♭–G–B♭, about a semitone above D–F♯–A; the cause is unestablished.

transitions.title: The instruments continue beyond the final words
transitions.how: The voice finishes while the rocking figure continues in the inner strings. Horn and bassoon lines take the foreground above divided lower strings, and the postlude gradually spreads the closing motion across the ensemble. The written D-major centre remains in place as the texture and dynamics diminish; the ending prolongs arrival rather than starting another stanza.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 84–86, rehearsal 10 and close. The report records very low onset density from 4:30 and a quieter sustained span after 5:05. This approximate boundary does not identify the precise last word. Key names describe the written score: this transfer’s final pitch classes are E♭–G–B♭, about a semitone above D–F♯–A; the cause is unestablished.

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song V, printed pp. 60–86; written pitch is not assumed to equal this transfer’s playback pitch; passage-level scoring, not an instantaneous list of sounding parts. Timings are provisional score proportions checked against the recording’s level changes; no bar alignment or aural verification.

timeline.note: Opening storm: short wind figures, muted strings, tremolo cellos and accented harp chords.
Storm stanzas: the singer declaims amid continuing wind and string agitation.
Transition passage: a held high piccolo tone, small-bell notes and thinning string figures replace the crowded storm texture.
Lullaby passage: the voice and quiet strings unfold above the celesta’s rocking figure; most winds withdraw.
Postlude: the voice drops out; horn and bassoon lines continue above moving inner strings.
Closing passage: sustained wind harmony and diminishing string and celesta figures carry the final release.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
